interactions.label: Why does every form of glaucoma ultimately raise intraocular pressure?

params.question: Why does every form of glaucoma ultimately raise intraocular pressure?

answers.text: Each type increases aqueous humour production by the ciliary body

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Aqueous production by the ciliary body remains relatively constant across all glaucoma types. The problem is always impaired drainage, not overproduction.

answers.text: Each type causes inflammation that collapses Schlemm's canal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While some secondary glaucomas involve inflammation, the mechanism varies widely — congenital glaucoma involves maldevelopment, POAG involves gradual matrix accumulation, and angle-closure involves mechanical obstruction. None is primarily inflammatory.

answers.text: Each type disrupts aqueous outflow at a specific point along the drainage pathway

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Whether the obstruction is at the trabecular meshwork, the iridocorneal angle, or elsewhere, every form of glaucoma raises IOP by impairing outflow rather than increasing production.

answers.text: Each type obstructs the uveoscleral drainage route exclusively

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The uveoscleral route handles only 10–15% of total drainage. Most glaucoma types primarily affect the conventional trabecular meshwork pathway, and the specific site of obstruction varies by type.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle is that IOP reflects the balance between aqueous production and outflow. In every form of glaucoma, production remains relatively constant — the problem is always impaired drainage at a specific point along the outflow pathway.

Exactly right. IOP reflects the balance between aqueous production and outflow. In glaucoma, production stays constant — the problem is always impaired drainage at some point along the outflow pathway.

interactions.label: Why is surgery the first-line treatment for congenital glaucoma, unlike adult op

params.question: Why is surgery the first-line treatment for congenital glaucoma, unlike adult open-angle glaucoma where drops come first?

answers.text: No drop can correct a trabecular meshwork that never formed properly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The fundamental defect is trabeculodysgenesis — the drainage tissue arrested during foetal development. Goniotomy or trabeculotomy surgically opens this dysplastic meshwork. Drops like timolol serve only as a bridge to the operating theatre.

answers.text: Topical drops cannot penetrate the immature infant cornea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Topical drops can penetrate the infant cornea — timolol and dorzolamide are used as a temporary bridge before surgery. The real reason is that drops treat functional obstruction, not a structural developmental anomaly.

answers.text: Infants cannot tolerate the systemic side-effects of glaucoma drops

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While systemic absorption is a concern in infants, drops like timolol are safely used short-term as a bridge to surgery. The real reason is that no medication can create drainage tissue that was never formed.

answers.text: Surgery is preferred because it avoids general anaesthesia in infants

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both goniotomy and trabeculotomy actually require general anaesthesia in infants. Surgery is chosen because the structural anomaly — undeveloped trabecular meshwork — can only be corrected surgically, not pharmacologically.

overallFeedback.feedback: The reason is structural: congenital glaucoma results from trabeculodysgenesis, meaning the drainage tissue never matured during foetal development. No medication can create tissue that was never formed — only surgery (goniotomy or trabeculotomy) can establish drainage.

Precisely. Congenital glaucoma results from trabeculodysgenesis — angle tissue that never matured. No medication can build tissue that was never formed, making surgical correction the only definitive treatment.

interactions.label: What fundamentally distinguishes secondary glaucoma from primary glaucoma?

params.question: What fundamentally distinguishes secondary glaucoma from primary glaucoma?

answers.text: Secondary glaucoma always presents with higher intraocular pressures than primary glaucoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IOP can be extremely high in both categories — acute primary angle-closure can reach 50–80 mmHg. Peak pressure does not distinguish secondary from primary glaucoma.

answers.text: Secondary glaucoma only obstructs an open angle, never a closed one

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Secondary glaucoma can affect either mechanism. Pseudoexfoliation and pigment clog an open angle, while neovascular membranes and posterior synechiae can close the angle.

answers.text: Secondary glaucoma does not damage the optic nerve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both primary and secondary glaucoma damage the optic nerve through raised IOP. The difference lies in whether the underlying cause is identifiable, not in the end-organ damage.

answers.text: Secondary glaucoma has an identifiable underlying cause, and treating it may resolve the glaucoma entirely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Whether it is pseudoexfoliation material, pigment granules, steroids, or a swollen lens — identifying and treating the cause may resolve the pressure elevation entirely, unlike primary glaucoma which requires lifelong control.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction: in secondary glaucoma, the elevated pressure always has an identifiable underlying cause. Treating that cause — stopping steroids, extracting a swollen lens, managing retinal ischaemia — may resolve the glaucoma entirely, unlike primary glaucoma which needs lifelong control.
Exactly. The hallmark of secondary glaucoma is an identifiable, treatable cause. Treating that cause alongside urgent IOP reduction is the dual-track principle covered in this section.

interactions.label: A 58-year-old patient with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma says, 'My vision

params.question: A 58-year-old patient with newly diagnosed open-angle glaucoma says, 'My vision is perfectly fine — why should I use drops every day for the rest of my life?' Which response best addresses this concern?

answers.text: Your drops will gradually improve your vision over the coming months

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Glaucoma drops do not improve existing vision. Their purpose is entirely preventive — protecting remaining vision from further irreversible optic nerve damage. Setting a false expectation of improvement is the commonest cause of early discontinuation.

answers.text: Your vision feels fine because glaucoma destroys peripheral vision silently — the drops prevent further irreversible loss of the vision you still have

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This addresses the root misconception: the patient feels no benefit because glaucoma is silent. Framing treatment as protecting existing vision — not curing disease — is the single most important message for long-term adherence.

answers.text: You are right that treatment can wait safely until you begin to notice symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This is dangerous advice. By the time a patient with open-angle glaucoma notices visual loss, significant irreversible optic nerve damage has already occurred. Treatment must begin before symptoms appear.

answers.text: The drops are mainly for the redness and discomfort that will develop later

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chronic open-angle glaucoma typically causes neither redness nor discomfort. The drops target intraocular pressure to prevent silent, progressive optic nerve damage — not symptoms the patient might eventually feel.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical counselling message: glaucoma drops are preventive, not curative. They protect remaining vision from further irreversible optic nerve damage. Framing treatment as protection — not cure — is the key to long-term adherence.

Well done. The most important counselling message: these drops protect the vision you still have — they do not restore what is lost. Like hypertension, glaucoma is silent and requires preventive treatment before damage becomes apparent.
